title: The Son of the Brahmin

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha, a gifted Brahmin's son loved by everyone, including his devoted friend Govinda, feels that the teachings and rituals of his elders have not given him inner peace. He asks his father for permission to join the wandering ascetics called Samanas; his father refuses, but Siddhartha stands silently all night until his father consents. Govinda goes with him.

vocabulary.definition: The act of washing or cleansing
vocabulary.context: The evening had come, it was time to perform the evening’s ablution.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ablution”: ab- (Latin ab, "away from"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: (Opt.) A point in which the rays of light meet, after being reflected or refrcted, and at which the image is formed
vocabulary.context: Siddhartha sat there lost in thought, his eyes were rigidly focused towards a very distant target, the tip of his tongue was protruding a little between the teeth, he seemed not to breathe.

vocabulary.definition: Extremely rigid in self-denial and devotions

vocabulary.definition: Belonging to the earliest period or state

vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The act or form of calling for the assistance or presence of some superior being
vocabulary.context: The sacrifices and the invocation of the gods were excellent—but was that all?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “invocation”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + voc (Latin vocare, "to call") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To take a part, portion, lot, or share, in common with others
vocabulary.context: For a long time, Siddhartha had been partaking in the discussions of the wise men, practising debate with Govinda, practising with Govinda the art of reflection, the service of meditation.

vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Marked with the sign of the cross
vocabulary.context: As he slowly left on stiff legs in the first light of day the still quiet town, a shadow rose near the last hut, who had crouched there, and joined the pilgrim—Govinda.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “crouched”: -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Behind them blew a hot scent of quiet passion, of destructive service, of merciless self-denial.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “merciless”: -less (Old English -leas, "without"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Brahmins were the priestly caste in ancient India; the Upanishads and the idea of Atman (the inner self) shape Siddhartha's questions. Hesse, a German writer, studied Indian thought and wrote during the years after World War I.

significance: The opening establishes the novel's central pattern: knowledge received from teachers cannot replace knowledge gained by living.
discussionQuestions: Why isn't Siddhartha satisfied, even though he is admired and successful?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the search for self-knowledge?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “The Son of the Brahmin,” how does Hesse show restlessness despite privilege? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Son of the Brahmin develops the idea of restlessness despite privilege. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses characterization in The Son of the Brahmin to complicate the reader's understanding of restlessness despite privilege. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Son of the Brahmin within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of restlessness despite privilege responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Son of the Brahmin as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of restlessness despite privilege. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

satQuestions.passage: After the usual time of the exercise in meditation had passed, Govinda rose. The evening had come, it was time to perform the evening’s ablution. He called Siddhartha’s name. Siddhartha did not answer. Siddhartha sat there lost in thought, his eyes were rigidly focused towards a very distant target, the tip of his tongue was protruding a little between the teeth, he seemed not to breathe. Thus sat he, wrapped up in contemplation, thinking Om, his soul sent after the Brahman as an arrow.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why isn't Siddhartha satisfied, even though he is admired and successful? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are ablution, focused, ascetics, pristine, invocation. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “The evening had come, it was time to perform the evening’s ablution.” Webster's says: The act of washing or cleansing. Now the word history: “ablution”: ab- (Latin ab, "away from"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “focus”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “ascetic”: as- (Latin ad, "to") + -ic (Greek -ikos, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Brahmins were the priestly caste in ancient India; the Upanishads and the idea of Atman (the inner self) shape Siddhartha's questions. Hesse, a German writer, studied Indian thought and wrote during the years after World War I. Why does this chapter matter? The opening establishes the novel's central pattern: knowledge received from teachers cannot replace knowledge gained by living. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to restlessness despite privilege.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Setting, Symbolism.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the search for self-knowledge? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.
